title: Gratitude

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: savlanut, patience, from a root about carrying a load. Your line was bear it. Which delay did you carry? Today, noticing who carried things for you. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-eight.

Two guests leave the same dinner party. In the car, the first one says: did you see how much work went into that? The bread was homemade. She set a place card with my name. She stayed up cooking for us. The second one says: honestly, it was just pasta. I had one glass of wine. They'd have made dinner anyway. Same table, same food, same host. The Talmud tells a version of this story, two guests and two ways of leaving, and the difference between them has a name. That name is today's word.
screen: `TWO GUESTS, ONE DINNER.` → `LOOK HOW MUCH WORK WENT IN.` → `IT WAS JUST PASTA.`

segments.voice: Hakarat hatov. Recognizing the good. Turn it four ways. First, the phrase. It doesn't say feeling thankful. It says recognizing, the way you recognize a face in a crowd. The good is already there; the work is to see it, and to see who did it. Second, the two guests. In tractate Berakhot, the sage Ben Zoma describes them. The good guest says, in effect: how much trouble my host went to, and all of it for me. The bad guest says: what trouble did he go to? I ate one piece of bread, one cup of wine, and whatever he did, he did for his own household. The meal didn't change. The seeing did. Third, a word that some teachers say means two things. The Hebrew word for giving thanks, hodaah, can also mean admitting, as in admitting a fact. The short prayer some Jews say on waking begins modeh ani, I thank, or I acknowledge. Gratitude, in this language, is a kind of confession: I didn't do this alone. Someone set the table. Fourth, people, not only God. Jewish prayer thanks God often. Mussar adds that hakarat hatov points at people too: the parent who drove you, the teacher who stayed late, the stranger who held the door. Earlier this week a rabbi measured his water so a water-carrier would carry less. Hakarat hatov is the other side of that story: noticing the buckets someone carried for you, and saying so. The second guest isn't a villain. He's just tired, and a little proud, and not looking. Mussar asks for the first guest's eyes, one dinner at a time.
screen: `RECOGNIZE, LIKE A FACE IN A CROWD.` · `BEN ZOMA'S TWO GUESTS.` · `MODEH: I THANK, I ADMIT.` · `PEOPLE, NOT ONLY GOD.` · then, large: `RECOGNIZE THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name three good things done for you. Settle, and breathe. Look back over the last day or two, like the good guest in the car. Find one thing someone did for you that you barely noticed. Name it, and name who did it. Then a second. Maybe the person who made your coffee, or the friend who texted to check in. Then a third, maybe from long ago: someone who taught you to read, or to drive, or to cook. For each one, picture the effort it took them. Not just the gift. The trouble. If you pray, you can give thanks for them in your own words. If you don't, simply hold each face for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Hakarat hatov. Recognizing the good: seeing what someone did for you, and the trouble it took, like Ben Zoma's good guest. Today's word.
Your line: recognize the good. Today, tell one person exactly what they did for you and what it took them, in one specific sentence. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: In Mussar practice, Jews work on hakarat hatov by noticing and naming specific kindnesses from other people, and the short morning prayer modeh ani begins the day with thanks.

'Some Jews say modeh ani on waking' kept deliberately vague; confirm.
